subtitle: Curiosity is a skill you can practice. Ask purposeful questions, listen for meanings you may have missed and choose a responsible response, without making people explain their whole lives.
scope: For staff across DHS. Original practice explores curiosity as a professional skill and as a source of personal understanding. Private, unrecorded reflection and the practice path are equally legitimate. Relevant questions do not authorize medical inquiry, personal diagnosis, group profiling or decisions outside assigned authority. Actual equity-analysis and reporting duties remain applicable. Native American- and Tribal-specific matters are referred to the appropriate office within ADSA.
introTranscript: Curiosity is useful when it helps you notice the question you have not yet asked. It can also become intrusive if someone must satisfy your interest before receiving a respectful response. This course follows Casey and Drew, who attach different meanings to asking questions before offering an idea. A separate DHS feedback example shows how inquiry can inform practical action. You may use an example throughout or reflect privately without entering personal details.

intro.heading: Give curiosity a useful purpose
intro.body:
The Council of Europe’s conceptual account of intercultural learning connects openness, curiosity and questioning familiar assumptions. It also recognizes self-understanding. Those ideas inform the original exercises here, not a new DHS procedure or a requirement that anyone explain personal affiliations.

Casey and Drew are planning a small neighborhood reading event. Casey offers an idea immediately to show enthusiasm. Drew first asks what the host hopes the event will achieve. Casey interprets the question as resistance. Drew later volunteers a learned meaning: asking about the purpose before offering an idea shows that the host’s intention matters.

The contrast is not simply that Casey talks and Drew asks questions. It concerns different expressions of respect: initiative can convey investment to Casey, while purposeful inquiry conveys regard to Drew. Casey’s first interpretation missed that meaning. A curious response can examine the question rather than classify Drew as difficult.

You can understand the practice contrast without contacting a colleague or producing a work result. In professional use, the inquiry should relate to the task and its actual responsibilities. Curiosity is not permission to collect personal history just because it might be interesting.

flashcards.back: Purposeful inquiry that improves understanding relevant to your work while respecting choice, privacy and actual responsibilities.
What is actually known about an event before a motive or meaning is added.
A proposed interpretation that needs examination rather than being treated as the event itself.
A question whose purpose is understandable and whose optional personal parts can be declined.
Considering what the person’s account changes in your understanding rather than only collecting words.
A privacy, authority, time or task boundary that should be explained honestly rather than bypassed through curiosity.

items.title: Find the unanswered meaning
items.body: Casey knows that Drew asked about purpose. Casey does not yet know that the question rejects the event. Naming this gap makes a useful inquiry possible. It also prevents a routine behavior from becoming a character judgment before the person has had room to explain it.

items.title: Purpose keeps the question proportionate
items.body: A question about what Drew meant in this exchange can clarify the interaction. A demand to explain every family or community influence is much larger than the task needs. Curiosity becomes more useful when the learner can say why the question matters and what it need not reveal.

items.title: Personal insight can be enough
items.body: Casey may realize that immediate initiative has a learned meaning of care. That insight is worthwhile even without changing an event plan. Comparing it with Drew’s meaning can broaden self-understanding while leaving both people free to keep an honest preference.

tabs.label: Label first
tabs.body: Casey calls Drew resistant because the question interrupted the flow. The label fills an unknown meaning with a judgment. It makes later explanation easier to dismiss and changes the relationship before the actual purpose of the question is understood.

tabs.label: Ask for everything
tabs.body: Casey requests Drew’s entire cultural background to explain the question. This exceeds the relevant interaction and may pressure disclosure. A smaller inquiry about this moment can be clearer and does not require a personal biography.

tabs.label: Ask about this moment
tabs.body: Casey asks whether the question was intended to clarify the host’s purpose. Drew can confirm, correct or decline the optional explanation. The inquiry can revise Casey’s interpretation without demanding a group identity or claiming that one answer explains everyone.

check.question: What is a useful purpose for curiosity here?
check.correct: Clarify the meaning of Drew’s question rather than treat it as resistance or demand a personal history.
wrong: Require Drew to prove the question came from an authentic tradition.
Collect private stories to make the event planning feel inclusive.
check.feedbackCorrect: A relevant question addresses the actual interpretive gap. It can improve understanding without a diagnosis, authenticity test or unnecessary collection.
check.feedbackIncorrect: The exchange cannot determine an individual orientation. Authenticity proof and collecting private stories turn inquiry into a personal demand. The useful question is what this particular contribution meant and what it changes in Casey’s interpretation.

items.text: Drew asked what the host wanted the event to achieve.
Drew may associate inquiry with respecting the host’s purpose.
Explain your entire background before we can respond.
Casey offered an idea immediately.
Casey may associate initiative with enthusiasm.
Prove your practice is culturally authentic.

intro.heading: Separate observation from the story you added
intro.body:
Casey notices that Drew asks about purpose twice during the event planning. Casey’s story grows: Drew must distrust the host. Another explanation is possible: Drew may be trying to align ideas with the host’s intention. A repeated question does not settle which account fits.

Separating observation and interpretation does not mean pretending that patterns never matter. It means describing the pattern accurately and not adding a motive it cannot establish. “Drew asked about purpose twice” can be known in the example. “Drew distrusts the host” remains an interpretation.

A curious question might ask what remains unclear about the purpose. If Drew volunteers the respect meaning, Casey can reconsider the distrust story. If Drew identifies a practical ambiguity instead, the response should fit that information. Cultural learning should not force every unclear moment into a cultural explanation.

You can also examine your own story privately. Why did repetition feel like distrust to Casey? Perhaps Casey learned that asking again signals doubt. That possibility helps examine the reaction without diagnosing Casey or declaring the learned meaning wrong.

Identify what a relevant question could clarify.
What should Casey do instead?
lessons.keyStatement: Keep an interpretation open until relevant information supports it.

items.title: Describe the repetition accurately
items.body: Twice is a feature of the practice event, not proof of a stable trait. Recording or thinking about the actual behavior can make the question clearer. It avoids the leap from a pattern in one activity to a permanent judgment about the person.

items.title: Alternatives are not conclusions
items.body: The respect explanation is a possibility until Drew supplies relevant information. It should not replace the distrust story as another certainty. Generating alternatives is useful because it reveals the inquiry needed, not because the learner can guess a kinder motive and stop there.

items.title: Consider your own interpretive habit
items.body: Casey may have learned that repeated questions challenge confidence. Recognizing this can explain the reaction without excusing an unsupported judgment. Personal understanding can remain private, and Casey can still ask the task question without explaining the whole personal history.

tabs.label: Negative certainty
tabs.body: Casey concludes the repeated question proves distrust. The interpretation may feel plausible, but the count alone does not establish it. Acting on that certainty can exclude Drew’s contribution before the actual concern is understood.

tabs.label: Positive certainty
tabs.body: Casey decides Drew must be showing respect because that is a kinder interpretation. This also decides a meaning without information. A favorable stereotype still makes the person’s account unnecessary and can miss a real practical concern.

tabs.label: A clear open question
tabs.body: Casey asks what about the purpose remains unresolved. Drew can describe a meaning or an information gap. The response can then fit the actual explanation rather than the learner’s preferred story.

check.question: What does Drew’s repeated question establish?
check.correct: The question was repeated; the motive or meaning still needs relevant information.
wrong: Drew certainly follows a fixed cultural script of respect.
Repetition makes inquiry about the task unnecessary.
check.feedbackCorrect: A known pattern can inform a question without settling the motive. Both positive and negative certainty exceed what the repetition establishes.
check.feedbackIncorrect: The count does not prove distrust or a cultural script. Repetition can make a clarification useful rather than unnecessary. State the observed pattern and ask what remains unclear without treating your guess as the person’s explanation.

items.text: Drew asked about purpose twice.
Drew may be showing regard for the host’s intention.
What about the purpose remains unclear?
Drew must distrust the host.
The question concerned the event’s intended result.
Would an explanation of the host’s aim help?

scenario.context: DHS practice case: Casey wants to replace the distrust story with certainty that Drew’s repeated question is a cultural expression of respect.
options: Record the favorable explanation as fact.
Keep both interpretations open and ask about the unresolved purpose.
Ignore the question because any repetition is inappropriate.
responses: A favorable guess still needs relevant information.
This uses alternatives to support inquiry rather than to decide the person’s meaning.
That imposes a rule not established in the situation.

lessons.transfer: Privately separate one practice event from two interpretations. You may examine why one story feels familiar without recording personal details.

move.control: You can describe a pattern and its unknown meaning accurately.
move.failure: A kinder guess replaces a harsh guess but remains untested certainty.
move.next: Use alternatives to identify the next relevant question.

intro.heading: Invite an answer without making disclosure the price
intro.body:
Casey asks Drew, “Would you like to explain what asking about the purpose means to you, or should we just clarify the event’s aim?” The question offers two relevant paths. Drew can contribute a personal meaning without making it necessary for the planning to continue.

This differs from an invitation that quietly carries a penalty: explain your background or your question will not be taken seriously. A person may prefer to discuss the practical issue without describing its origins. Their choice not to disclose is not proof that the concern is insincere.

In DHS work, optional cultural reflection should also remain distinct from information required by an authorized process. Staff should not promise that every question is optional when an actual duty requires particular work information. Explain the real purpose and handling rather than use a learning invitation to disguise a requirement.

If a person states a disability-related employment need, follow the actual accommodation route. MMB Policy 1433 does not permit supervisors or managers to request medical information or documentation; appropriate documentation questions belong to the ADA Coordinator. Curiosity about meaning cannot become an informal exception to that rule.

Distinguish optional personal sharing from information required by an actual work process.

lessons.keyStatement: Ask only what fits the purpose and be honest about what is optional.

items.title: Offer a useful alternative
items.body: Clarifying the host’s aim lets the task proceed even if Drew keeps the personal meaning private. The alternative is relevant rather than a token choice. It shows that disclosure is not the price of being heard.

items.title: Do not punish a declined invitation
items.body: Casey can accept “I would rather just discuss the plan” and continue with the purpose question. Pressing for the hidden reason would make the invitation less voluntary. The declined account leaves a personal meaning unknown without invalidating the task concern.

items.title: Keep formal inquiry in its real role
items.body: A supervisor may need to describe the actual work and forward a request promptly. That is different from asking for a diagnosis to satisfy curiosity. The coordinator’s appropriate documentation role and agency process remain intact; optional cultural learning grants no new medical authority.

tabs.label: A disguised demand
tabs.body: Casey says sharing is voluntary but stops planning until Drew explains a background. The words and consequence conflict. Such an invitation can pressure someone to provide a story they did not choose to share.

tabs.label: An unlimited promise
tabs.body: A staff member says every work question is optional and all information will always remain private. That can conflict with actual duties or required reporting. Respect requires an honest scope, not a promise beyond the role.

tabs.label: A scoped invitation
tabs.body: Casey explains why the meaning may help, offers the practical path and accepts a decline. In actual work, the person also receives a truthful explanation of any required process. This distinguishes learning choice from operational responsibility.

check.question: Drew declines the personal explanation but asks to clarify the host’s aim. What should Casey do?
check.correct: Accept the choice and address the relevant purpose question without treating privacy as insincerity.
wrong: Stop planning until Drew shares a personal history.
Assume the question had no real basis.
Promise all future work information will be optional.
check.feedbackCorrect: The practical path was a real alternative. Accepting it keeps the personal account voluntary and the task useful.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Stopping planning makes disclosure a condition. Declining personal explanation does not prove insincerity, and optional learning cannot make every future work duty optional. Use the relevant practical path and be honest about actual requirements.

items.text: Would you like to explain the meaning, or just clarify the purpose?
An appropriate accommodation documentation question belongs to the ADA Coordinator.
Planning stops until you reveal your background.
We can keep the personal explanation private and discuss the task.
The recipient promptly forwards a request and tells the person the decision-maker under Policy 1433.
Prove a diagnosis to a curious supervisor.

lessons.transfer: Practice the practice invitation privately. No personal explanation needs to be entered; actual work information follows its applicable requirements.

move.failure: An optional invitation hides a disclosure demand or promises more than the role allows.

intro.heading: Listen for what changes your understanding
intro.body:
Drew chooses to explain: asking about purpose shows that the host’s intention is worth understanding before suggesting a direction. Casey realizes the question was not simply hesitation. It conveyed a form of respect. Casey’s own quick initiative conveyed another form: willingness to contribute energy.

A useful summary might be, “You want the idea to respond to the host’s aim before choosing it.” Drew can correct that summary. Casey need not repeat a personal account in public or declare that all future suggestions require this order.

The clarified meaning can change Casey’s response: explain the aim, invite a question and then offer the same honest idea as a possibility. This is more than adding polite words. It gives regard for the host’s purpose a practical place in the conversation while retaining Casey’s initiative.

Listening does not require accepting every requested action. If the event has a real limit, explain it and examine feasible choices. Respect for Drew’s account and responsibility for the task can coexist. The personal learning may also remain internal without a later action.

inThisLesson: Identify how a volunteered meaning revises a first interpretation.
Distinguish listening from waiting to defend your original position.
Develop a response connected to the clarified meaning.

lessons.keyStatement: Let the answer inform the response rather than merely finish the question.

items.title: The answer revises a specific inference
items.body: Casey originally read resistance. Drew’s account supplies a different meaning. Casey can reconsider that inference without claiming complete understanding of Drew’s life or rejecting every instance in which repeated questions might signal doubt. The conclusion stays with this exchange.

items.title: Check the summary
items.body: A concise summary lets Drew correct what Casey heard. It should concern the relevant meaning rather than label Drew. “You need the aim clarified” is a checkable account; “You are a cautious cultural type” assigns a category that the exchange cannot establish.

items.title: Connect meaning and action
items.body: Explaining the aim before offering the idea gives Drew’s respect meaning a place in the response. Casey still contributes honestly. The adjustment is culturally informed by the account, not a performance copied from an assumed group script. Its effect remains a separate question.

tabs.label: Wait to defend
tabs.body: Casey hears Drew’s words only to prepare reasons why quick ideas are efficient. The response may defend a real value, but it misses what the explanation changes. The question then becomes a detour before the original conclusion.

tabs.label: Agree automatically
tabs.body: Casey announces that Drew’s approach must always be used. This replaces one default with another and may create an unsupported rule. Listening can inform a suitable choice without granting unlimited control or abandoning other relevant purposes.

tabs.label: Summarize and respond
tabs.body: Casey checks the purpose-focused meaning, explains the aim and offers the idea in that context. Drew’s account can now shape the response while Casey retains initiative. No claim is made about everyone’s preferences or an assured outcome.

check.question: What shows that Casey used the answer?
check.correct: Casey checks the clarified meaning and gives it a relevant place in the response.
wrong: Casey labels Drew as a cautious cultural type.
Casey declares Drew’s approach mandatory in every future task.
Casey repeats the question but ignores the answer.
check.feedbackCorrect: The response connects the actual meaning to a suitable choice while allowing correction and preserving other relevant values.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A cultural-type label is unsupported, a universal rule overextends the account, and an ignored answer leaves inquiry performative. Use the actual clarification to reconsider the interpretation and choose a fitting response.

items.text: Drew associates purpose questions with regard for the host.
Casey checks whether the summary fits.
Everyone with Drew’s background follows this order.
Casey associates immediate initiative with contribution.
Casey explains the aim before offering the idea.
The explanation proves all later interactions will improve.

lessons.transfer: Privately summarize the practice meaning and a possible response. If using your own value, keep its origins private and any application optional.

move.control: You can let new information revise the inference and response.
move.failure: A question collects words while the original judgment remains untouched.
move.next: Check the relevant summary and choose a response it genuinely informs.

intro.heading: Use inquiry in actual work without avoiding responsibility
intro.body:
In a separate practice DHS feedback discussion, participant Lee says a service letter gives a next step but does not explain what will happen after it. Staff member Quinn initially sees a complete instruction: the address and action are present. Lee volunteers another meaning of trust: an institution’s request feels more accountable when the person understands what follows and who will respond.

The concern is not automatically low literacy, distrust of all government or a group trait. Lee has identified a specific information gap and a meaning of accountability. Quinn can examine whether the letter’s next-step explanation is accurate and sufficient for this task.

A relevant question asks which part of the following process is unclear. It does not require Lee to disclose service history or represent everyone. Quinn remains responsible for checking the actual process and preparing any authorized revision. Consultant guidance can support this reasoning without becoming a required gate or doing the staff work.

Inquiry also has limits. A protected-class allegation raised to a manager requires immediate HR or agency Affirmative Action Officer reporting under Policy 1436. Optional questions about cultural meaning must not delay that duty. Required DHS equity analysis and authorized decisions remain applicable to the actual policy or service work; a reflective discussion is not their replacement.

Distinguish inquiry from an excuse to delay required action.
Identify a next step within actual staff responsibility and authority.
What should the manager do?
lessons.keyStatement: Use inquiry to improve the response, not postpone the duty.

items.title: The meaning changes what completion means
items.body: Quinn had checked whether an action was stated. Lee’s account raises the following process and accountability. That does not prove the whole letter is inequitable, but it gives Quinn a more relevant question than whether the participant can read the instruction.

items.title: Ask about the gap, not the whole person
items.body: Which next step remains unclear can help Quinn examine the work. Asking why people like Lee distrust government would impose a group premise and invite a broad story not supplied in the account. Curiosity is useful when it stays connected to the question being addressed.

items.title: Prepare within actual authority
items.body: Quinn can verify the process and propose a truthful explanation through the appropriate review. Quinn cannot invent a response deadline, promise service eligibility or change policy independently. A specific contribution informs the work without supplying authority for unsupported commitments.

tabs.label: Explain harder
tabs.body: Quinn repeats the address more forcefully because the instruction seems complete. This answers the original reading but ignores the newly described gap. It risks treating the participant as the problem when the question concerns what follows the stated action.

tabs.label: Ask for a life story
tabs.body: Quinn seeks Lee’s whole service history to understand trust. That expands a specific concern into a disclosure demand. The actual next-step question may be addressed without those details, and the participant may prefer to keep them private.

tabs.label: Check the actual next step
tabs.body: Quinn asks what remains unclear, verifies the process and prepares a relevant explanation within authority. This lets the contributed meaning affect the response. Its usefulness still needs appropriate review rather than a claim that every participant will trust the institution.

check.question: What does Lee’s feedback justify?
check.correct: Examine the actual next-step explanation and accountability question without a group inference or unauthorized promise.
wrong: Assume everyone in Lee’s community distrusts government.
Promise a deadline before checking the service process.
Make Lee responsible for rewriting all service letters.
check.feedbackCorrect: The account identifies a relevant question for staff work. It does not establish population attitudes, create authority or transfer responsibility.
check.feedbackIncorrect: One account cannot show every community member’s attitude. An unchecked deadline is an unsupported promise, and the participant need not own staff revisions. Use the contribution to examine the actual process through assigned responsibility.

items.text: Lee wants to understand what follows the stated step.
Quinn verifies the actual service process.
Lee must rewrite all service communications.
Lee links a clear following process with accountability.
A manager immediately reports a protected-class allegation under Policy 1436.
The feedback proves every community member shares one attitude.

intro.heading: Know what the question actually accomplished
intro.body:
Casey can say the purpose question gained a new meaning and the resistance story was reconsidered. That is an actual learning result in the practice path. Asking three questions alone would not establish it. A question can be irrelevant, pressured or ignored after it is answered.

Quinn can say the letter’s next-step gap was identified and a revised explanation prepared for proper review. Whether the explanation helps the intended task remains a different question. A participant’s thank-you may show appreciation without proving universal trust or service access. No new feedback leaves the effect unknown.

A proportionate next step fits the question and authority. Casey may continue private reflection, with no entered note or real action. Quinn may use an appropriate task review and protect personal information rather than collect broad sensitive histories merely to demonstrate rigor.

Professional curiosity remains a skill to practice, not a claim to unlimited inquiry. Its quality depends on relevant purpose, openness to correction, respectful choice and a responsible response. You can return to those points when an unfamiliar meaning or unresolved task invites another question.

inThisLesson: Distinguish asking a question from learning or changing a response.
Describe missing evidence without inferring satisfaction or failure.
Choose a proportionate private or professional next step.
Which progress statement fits?
lessons.keyStatement: Judge inquiry by what became clearer, while keeping effect claims accurate.

items.title: Ask what became clearer
items.body: Casey understands that a purpose question can convey regard rather than resistance. That is more informative than a count of questions. The learning can be privately meaningful without needing a work report or an assessment of either person.

items.title: Describe the action accurately
items.body: Quinn prepared a revised explanation; that is useful work progress. It is not yet proof of the letter’s effect for every service user. Keeping the action’s scope accurate leaves room for an appropriate review without dismissing preparation as worthless.

items.title: Let uncertainty guide a suitable next step
items.body: If no task feedback exists, Quinn can name the unknown and identify the responsible review route. Missing information is neither reassurance nor automatic failure. It should not be filled with an invented story about why people did not respond.

tabs.label: Count questions
tabs.body: A learner celebrates asking many questions without considering their purpose or use. The count can reward intrusion or repeated asking just as easily as understanding. It does not show whether the answer revised an interpretation or informed a response.

tabs.label: Demand an outcome
tabs.body: A learner treats private insight as incomplete unless another person reports a benefit. This can pressure an unnecessary interaction or disclosure. Personal learning and professional effects are different results; only the latter needs a relevant task outcome claim.

tabs.label: Name the actual result
tabs.body: The learner identifies what was clarified, which response was prepared and what remains unknown. This gives each path a meaningful conclusion without mastery claims or false reassurance. A further question can be chosen only if it is useful and appropriate.

check.question: What best indicates useful inquiry in the practice cases?
check.correct: A relevant meaning or gap became clearer and informed understanding or a responsible response; any further effect remains separately examined.
wrong: The learner asked the highest number of questions.
Everyone thanked the learner, so all barriers disappeared.
Private insight was entered into a supervisor report.
check.feedbackCorrect: The result matches the inquiry’s purpose while separating understanding and action from unexamined effects. No question count or disclosure receipt substitutes for it.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A count does not establish quality. Gratitude does not prove all barriers disappeared, and entered reporting is not required for private insight. Name what actually became clearer and keep any further effect within the available evidence.

items.text: Casey reconsidered the resistance interpretation.
Quinn prepared an explanation for proper review.
An appropriate task review identifies which next-step information was usable.
More questions automatically mean better curiosity.
A relevant review documents an unresolved instruction gap.
No feedback proves universal satisfaction.

lessons.next: Use the job aid to keep curiosity purposeful, respectful and connected with responsible action.

scenario.context: DHS practice case: Quinn prepared a revised explanation, but no relevant task feedback is available yet. Casey gained a private insight through an example.
options: Nothing useful happened because there is no universal outcome.
All people will now trust the service.
Quinn prepared a response whose effect remains unknown; Casey’s insight is a legitimate learning result.
responses: Preparation and personal learning can each be useful without a universal outcome.
The available information does not support that prediction.
This values actual progress while leaving the separate effect open.

lessons.transfer: Privately identify what the practice inquiry clarified. Any work application should use relevant authorized evidence; no personal story or entered learning receipt is required.

move.control: You can distinguish a useful question, an actual insight and an unexamined effect.
move.failure: Counts, gratitude or missing feedback become proof of mastery or universal success.
move.next: Name the result you have and a relevant next question only if useful.

jobAid.subtitle: A short reminder for useful questions and responsible responses.
remember: Separate what happened from the meaning you supplied.
Ask for a relevant purpose, not a whole personal history.
Let an answer inform your understanding or response.
Private insight is worthwhile; professional effects require their own relevant evidence.

sections.heading: Before the question
items: What do I actually know, and what am I assuming?
What could this question clarify for the person, task or my own understanding?
Can the optional personal part be declined without penalty?

sections.heading: During the exchange
items: Explain the purpose and offer a relevant nonpersonal path where suitable.
Check the meaning heard rather than assign a group script.
Be honest about privacy, authority and actual requirements.
Do not use curiosity to request medical documents outside the proper role.

sections.heading: After the answer
items: Identify what changed in the interpretation or response.
Retain staff ownership and use required analysis, request or reporting routes.
State any missing evidence as unknown rather than reassurance or blame.
Choose a private, practice or proportionate work next step; no entered personal account is required.

sources.title: Council of Europe: Developing intercultural competence through education
sources.note: Conceptual discussion of openness, curiosity, questioning familiar assumptions and self-understanding. Original cases and inquiry routines here are not source exercises or new DHS procedures.

sources.title: Tervalon and Murray-García: Cultural humility versus cultural competence
sources.note: Historical medical-education concepts of ongoing reflection, listening and partnership. Clinical cases, statistics and historical mandates are not imported into DHS work.

sources.title: MMB Policy 1433: Reasonable accommodation
sources.note: Actual prompt forwarding and notice requirements, and the ADA Coordinator’s appropriate medical-documentation role. Supervisors and managers must not request medical information or documentation for accommodation.

sources.title: MMB Policy 1436: Harassment and discrimination prohibited
sources.note: Immediate manager and supervisor reporting to HR or the agency Affirmative Action Officer and actual assigned procedures. Optional inquiry does not delay that duty.

sources.title: DHS Equity Policy
sources.note: Actual equity-analysis expectations and formal requirements remain applicable. Learning routines support preparation rather than replace the authorized work.
